A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
patients with a strong sense of helplessness are more likely to benefit from CBT for insomnia.

patients who are highly cognitively distressed and who have a pronounced sense of helplessness about their insomnia may respond best to CBT, whereas those with a relatively more optimistic outlook may not.
CBT for insomnia is a powerful and efficacious treatment for patients who enter treatment with a strong sense of sleep-related self-efficacy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

patients with a pronounced sense that they cannot control their sleep (high DBAS scores) will benefit most from cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, whereas patients with less of a sense that they cannot sleep well (low DBAS scores) may be better served by other interventions.

patients with primary insomnia who are highly invested in the idea that they are helpless with regard to sleep and are convinced that they have a chronic sleep disorder are the ones who benefit most from CBT for insomnia.

the CBT treatment is more effective for patients who are highly convinced that their insomnia is due to factors beyond their control, and that they are not capable of changing the problem on their own.
